transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-12-07
Start: 15:00 PST
Duration: ~52 minutes
Location: Zoom
Attendees: Samira (Redwood AE), Diego (Redwood SE), Lena (Redwood Product), Anika (Helion CTO), James (Helion Sr ML Eng), Priya (Helion Infra)

Summary (auto): deep dive on GPU runtime behavior; compared TensorRT-LLM vs vLLM, discussed where CUDA graphs help/hurt, KV cache patterns, batching sweet spots, quantization/regression risk; next steps include joint benchmarks and sharing profiler artifacts.

Transcript:
[00:00] Samira: hey everyone, thanks for joining, we wanted to do a hands-on profiling session focused on GPU runtime stuff, kernel selection and how that interacts with batch size, cuda graphs, and the KV caching, is that the right agenda for you Anika?
[00:12] Anika: yep that sounds perfect, our main problem is we see big latency spikes when we hit long context chatty flows \u2014 throughput is ok but p95s are painful. we want to understand tradeoffs between using TensorRT-LLM optimized kernels vs vLLM for our LLMs.
[00:25] Diego: ok cool, quick intro \u2014 i'll show traces from our internal runs and then we can walk through your config. fair warning: some of the names in the exported traces are funky \u2014 the profiler sometimes says "TensorR-LLM" or "TRT LLM" so forgive the noise.
[00:38] James: hah yeah that's what we saw too, logs are not consistent. also small thing, we have quantized checkpoints (8-bit) and float16 variants; curious how kernel selection shifts.
[00:48] Priya: and on our side the constrant is that the staging runs have to be in our VPC and we need KMS key access \u2014 we'll need to validate the private deployment flow for the benchmark.
[00:58] Lena: noted \u2014 we'll provide the deploy scripts for VPC access and key routing.
[01:05] Diego: starting with kernel selection: core idea \u2014 TRT-LLM provides fused attention kernels and optimized GEMM paths for certain LLM shapes, but it's very shape-dependent. vLLM (and plain CUDA kernels) are more flexible but can pay in per-token throughput. i'll put up a trace now.
[01:22] [screen share starts \u2014 Diego sharing perf dashboard]
[01:30] Diego: here's a run on an MPT-style 8k sequence model, batch 1, seq len distribution around 1.2k tokens average \u2014 you'll see spikes at 1k and 4k boundaries because of kernel reconfig. the kernel selection table shows TRT picking a different fused kernel after token 1024 in our graph, which triggers a short stall while we rebuild cuGraph nodes.
[01:52] James: wait, rebuild cuGraph nodes? i thought cuda graphs were static once created. are you switching graphs mid-run?
[02:00] Diego: yeah so when sequence lengths cross thresholds or when kv-cache layout changes, the runtime is currently brittle \u2014 we try to reuse graphs but some ops get recompiled/retuned and that causes a micro-second to millisecond stall depending on fragmentation. in practice that's what pops p95s.
[02:18] Samira: just to be clear, these rebuilds are happening in TensorRT-LLM path more often because of fused kernel boundaries?
[02:25] Diego: exactly. TRT tends to have more specialized kernels that only apply in limited shapes, so when your distribution has many outlier lengths you get more churn. vLLM tends to choose more general kernels that are slower at steady-state but avoid rebuilds.
[02:40] Anika: is there a sweet spot where TRT is unequivocally better? like a particular batch size or sequence length profile?
[02:48] Diego: yes \u2014 TRT wins on throughput when sequence lengths are long and relatively uniform and batch sizes are moderate to large. e.g., batch 8, seq 4k with the same prompt shape consistently \u2014 TRT's fused attention + int8/float16 optimized GEMMs can give 1.6-2x token throughput. but if your workload is chatty with lots of short responses and lots of batch=1, TRT's kernel switching overhead can kill p95.
[03:10] James: that aligns with our telemetry \u2014 most of our production is chatty single-user flows, but we do have some high-throughput batched scoring for downstream indexing.
[03:18] Priya: also network overhead inside our VPC matters \u2014 we're not purely GPU bound for some routes; sometimes CPU serialization and grpc overhead show up as latency. any suggestions for isolating GPU stalls vs infra noise?
[03:29] Diego: instrumenting with nvprof/NSight helps, but we recommend a two-tier approach: 1) use kernel-level tracing (we'll share our nvtx/nvprof wrapper) to attribute time to kernels; 2) run a microbenchmark that pins only to the GPU (no network, same binary, local inputs) to get pure GPU behavior. then re-run with VPC invocation to measure infra delta.
[03:50] Samira: note: we'll provide the microbenchmark harness and a shared Datadog dashboard URL so you can correlate infra metrics.
[03:58] Anika: on KV cache \u2014 James noticed large memory churn when users switch contexts. is there a recommended pattern?
[04:06] Diego: yes, two things: prefix caching vs full KV retention. prefix caching (store only the last N tokens per session) reduces memory but can increase recompute on long-horizon sessions. also layout matters: contiguous KV blocks let TRT/Tensor cores use faster loads \u2014 fragmented KV (many small session caches) leads to many small memcpy operations. we see big perf wins by compacting session KV into per-device contiguous buffers and using async memcpy + pinned host staging.
[04:34] James: makes sense \u2014 our implementation keeps separate buffers per session, which probably fragments. we can change to a per-device pool. any gotchas?
[04:42] Diego: watch out for GC on the Python side if you're using a Python server; pinned memory lifetimes and PyTorch caching can be surprising. also quantization interacts with KV: int8 KV packing reduces memory but increases decode/encode cost on the host side.
[05:00] Anika: can we trust quantized models for quality? we have sensitive LLM features where hallucination costs money.
[05:06] Lena: we recommend doing evaluation runs with your eval suite \u2014 Redwood Optimize has a quantization suggestion tool but ultimately you need to validate on your prompts. small drop in ROUGE/EM is common at 8-bit, but many customers accept it for 2x cost reduction \u2014 others keep float16 for high-value routes.
[05:26] James: what's the overhead for enabling dynamic quantization paths? i.e. model serves float16 but falls back to float32 for certain tokens?
[05:34] Diego: dynamic precision switching is expensive \u2014 switching compute kernels mid-sequence triggers the same rebuild/retuning problem we discussed. better to pick a single compute profile per route and do routing by policy (route high-quality traffic to float16/float32 capacity, send bulk to int8).
[05:50] Priya: regarding on-prem deployment \u2014 we need to ensure KMS integration and that the control plane never exfiltrates keys. what's Redwood's private deployment model for the pilot?
[05:59] Samira: for pilots we have a private control plane option where the data plane runs in your VPC and keys stay in your KMS/HSM; Redwood gets only telemetry hashes. we'll send the architecture diagram and SOC2 details after the call.
[06:12] Anika: please do. also curious about GPU scheduler and priority for mixed workloads on a node. we run inference + some training infra on the same cluster.
[06:21] Diego: we recommend hard partitioning for predictable latency \u2014 dedicate GPUs for inference on dedicated capacity or use MIG if hardware supports it. mixing training and inference risks noisy neighbors. we can show scheduling configs for Dedicated pools.
[06:33] [crosstalk \u2014 background noise]
[06:40] James: back to CUDA graphs \u2014 you said earlier that we can sometimes reuse graphs. what's the recommended pattern to avoid rebuilds?
[06:47] Diego: create graphs for the 95th percentile shapes first. prewarm the graphs by running representative sequences; avoid creating graphs for rare outliers. also, when possible, use a batching strategy that pads sequences to power-of-two boundaries or to a small set of canonical lengths \u2014 that reduces kernel diversity.
[07:06] James: canonical lengths \u2014 does that add latency for short sequences because of padding?
[07:10] Diego: yes tradeoff \u2014 some wasted compute on tokens you don't need, but padding can reduce stalls and improve p95. we usually recommend a hybrid: for extremely latency-sensitive routes, keep batch=1 and lean kernels; for bulk scoring, use canonical batching.
[07:26] Anika: can Redwood runtime do automatic padding bucketing?
[07:30] Diego: yes, Redwood Optimize can suggest bucket boundaries based on your token distribution and we can configure runtime bucketing and batching rules. we'll export the suggested config.
[07:38] Priya: what about memory fragmentation over time \u2014 we've seen OOMs after long uptime. is there a recommended eviction strategy?
[07:46] Diego: use an LRU on session KV with a configurable max memory size, and a background compaction pass during low load. also watch allocator fragmentation \u2014 running a periodic warm restart or using a memory pool allocator helps.
[07:59] James: any specific kernel flags for TRT that we should set to avoid rebuilds?
[08:03] Diego: yes, pin the workspace sizes, disable autotune mid-run, and prebuild the int8 calibration caches. also ensure your TRT builder flags include deterministic optimization profiles if reproducibility is required. we'll add the exact flags to the shared doc.
[08:18] Anika: we also want to compare vLLM \u2014 we did some internal runs and saw vLLM had lower p95 but worse throughput on our heavy scoring jobs. curious what Redwood sees.
[08:29] Diego: that's consistent. vLLM's memory manager and batch scheduler are optimized for latency-first scenarios; it uses more generic kernels and fewer graph rebuilds. TensorRT gives big boost on throughput for long uniform workloads. the right answer can be hybrid: route latency-sensitive traffic to vLLM variants and throughput to TRT-optimized clusters.
[08:48] Samira: we do routing by policy today \u2014 you can pin routes by SLO tags.
[08:53] James: about profiling \u2014 what exact artifacts will you share?
[08:56] Diego: we'll share nvprof timeline exports, CUDA graph node dumps, kernel selection tables, a flamegraph-like kernel time breakdown, and the benchmark harness (dockerized). also a short runbook to reproduce the numbers.
[09:10] Priya: is there sensitive data in those traces? we can't share user prompts publicly.
[09:15] Diego: we recommend redacting prompts; the traces only need token lengths and op timings. we can run with synthetic inputs generated to match your length distributions \u2014 keep PII out.
[09:27] Anika: good. can we talk about deployment latency under VPC egress \u2014 sometimes NAT and ILB add 10-30ms.
[09:35] Diego: yes, place the data plane within your private subnets, use ENIs and local load balancers, and prefer unix socket or in-cluster gRPC where possible. we have a VPC reference architecture for minimal hop counts.
[09:49] James: and for A/B experiments between TRT and vLLM, how do you handle model weight parity? i.e. ensuring the same quantization and tokenization pipelines so we measure kernel differences not model differences.
[09:58] Lena: we usually recommend a freeze: same checkpoint, same tokenizer, same pre/post processors. then vary only runtime flags (TRT vs vLLM) and quantization. we can help generate a canonical test harness.
[10:12] Samira: ok time check \u2014 about 40 minutes in, let's go through concrete benchmark plan and owners.
[10:18] Diego: plan: 1) three workload profiles: chatty (batch1, avg len 200, many short turns), long-context (batch4, avg len 3.5k), bulk-scoring (batch16, seq 512). 2) run TRT-optimized binary and vLLM baseline on identical hardware (your 8xA100 staging). 3) collect kernel traces, NVTX, cuda graph dumps, and end-to-end p50/p95/p99, and token/s throughput. 4) evaluate with your eval prompts for quality diffs for quantized variants.
[10:45] James: timeline? we can provision cluster by Friday. can you share scripts asap so we can run early next week?
[10:52] Diego: yes we'll share by Thursday \u2014 i'll set the repo and invite you.
[10:56] Anika: any immediate red flags from what you saw in the sample telemetry we sent earlier?
[11:02] Diego: main red flag is the fragmentation in KV and frequent graph rebuilds due to many outlier sequence lengths. also mixing inference and training on same nodes \u2014 if you can't dedicate, consider MIG or strict capacity slices.
[11:14] Priya: understood. we'll try to isolate inference to dedicated nodes during the benchmark window.
[11:19] Samira: recap of action items: (1) Diego shares profiler scripts + repo; (2) Helion provisions staging and runs the three-profile benchmark; (3) Samira sends pilot contract & security docs. Everyone okay?
[11:30] Anika: yes. thanks team.
[11:33] James: thanks, looking forward to the artifacts.
[11:36] Samira: i'll follow up with calendar invite for the review week of 12/20. thanks all.
[11:42] [meeting ends]
